body: The spec contains an internal contradiction that undermines the research question itself. Linear, per-feature scaling (z-score, min-max, robust) is an affine transformation of location and scale; the t-statistic, one-way ANOVA F, and their p-values are invariant under such transformations by construction. The spec's own acceptance criteria acknowledge this: US-2 requires that 'the subsequent t-test p-value must remain consistent with the unscaled data (difference < 1e-4)'. If the pipeline must demonstrate p-value stability under scaling, then the simulation cannot find any effect of scaling on Type I error or power for these tests, and the mixed-effects model in FR-010 will necessarily find no fixed effect — making SC-007's framing ('must show a statistically significant fixed effect... if scaling impacts robustness') a criterion the design guarantees to fail. The only places where scaling could plausibly matter are (a) the chi-squared test on binned continuous data, where the choice of bin edges interacts with scaling — but the spec never states whether bins are fixed-width or quantile-based, which is the decisive design choice; and (b) numerical issues with outliers. Second, US-4 claims real-world datasets can 'validate the simulation findings,' but real data carry no known ground truth for the null or alternative, so Type I error and power cannot be measured there — only p-value agreement can be, which the spec elsewhere asserts is trivially preserved. Third, the Assumption section ties the ±0.005 margin of error to a '[deferred]' iteration count; for a binomial proportion at p≈0.05, that margin requires roughly n ≈ 7,300, so the 10,000-iteration figure in FR-004 is adequate, but the deferral leaves the sample-size justification formally incomplete. I would ask the authors to state explicitly what mechanism they hypothesize could make an affine rescaling alter a scale-invariant test statistic, and to specify the binning rule before any code is written.
